canonical_topic: What LNG Is and Why It Matters
definition: LNG is natural gas (methane) that has been cooled to roughly -260°F at normal atmospheric pressure so it condenses into a liquid, shrinking its volume to about 1/610th of the gaseous form.
core_idea: Because liquefied gas takes up so much less space, it can be economically loaded onto tanker ships and moved to places pipelines don't reach, turning a pipeline-bound commodity into something that can be shipped like oil.
key_points: Cooling to about -260°F at standard atmospheric pressure liquefies methane.
Liquefaction cuts the gas's volume to roughly 1/610th of its gaseous volume.
The compactness is what makes ship-based transport and non-traditional storage viable.
Small-scale (e.g., truck-based) LNG transport is still not cost-effective; the economics work at cargo-ship scale.
trading_implications: LNG lets producers reach overseas markets rather than being limited to whatever a pipeline connects to.
caveats: Small-scale/local LNG transport is not automatically cost-effective just because the gas is compact — ship-scale volumes are what make the economics work.
